item.title: Macro pulse: Europe's economy is losing steam but inflation won't let up
item.description:
The latest October PMI readings today don't paint a particularly encouraging picture of the health of the euro area economy. Growth is slowing and businesses are feeling the pinch, but inflation pressures are still refusing to go away. And that is the sort of headache that the ECB really doesn't need right now.

The data showed disappointing readings from both the manufacturing and services sectors, with the latter slowing rather markedly. A lot of that can be attributed to France though, as business activity there returned to contraction in October. And while Germany continues to hold up better, the broader slowdown across the region is becoming more difficult to ignore as we look to the final quarter this year.

With that in mind, this is where things get uncomfortable for the ECB. While business activity are showing signs of slowing down, price pressures haven't quite followed suit.

In looking at the chart above, businesses are still grappling with elevated cost pressures. The report noted that manufacturers saw a sharp acceleration in input prices in October, largely driven by higher energy costs, with the latest increase being the steepest since May.

The only consolation to this is that output price inflation did at least ease a little on the month. However, that could also be hinting that businesses may be finding it harder to pass rising costs on to consumers.

So, that is all leaving the ECB with quite the dilemma.

Traders are pricing in roughly 90% odds that the ECB will leave rates unchanged at next week's meeting. But looking to December, traders are still assigning around 68% odds of a rate hike in the final month of the year.

As things stand, inflation pressures remain the most pressing concern for policymakers. But then, the data today also serves up a reminder that the euro area economy isn't exactly in the best of shape to withstand further tightening. In particular, France is the big name that is struggling the most amid fiscal worries and concerns surrounding public finances. And the risk of spillover effects to the rest of the region should not be discounted.

Taking that into consideration, the big question isn't so much whether the ECB will hold next week. That's pretty much a done deal. Instead, it is whether policymakers can afford to keep raising rates if growth continues to lose momentum while higher energy costs squeeze businesses and households alongside growing fiscal worries across the region.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Crude oil extends gains as Saudi-Houthi conflict and concerns of US-Iran attacks keep the market supported
item.description:
The bullish momentum in crude oil has been slowly picking up after The New York Times reported that the US and Israeli militaries had developed plans for renewed strikes on Iran following the US midterm elections, with additional forces expected to be fully deployed by early November.

The Saudi-Houthi conflict, meanwhile, continues with the Houthis recently targeting Saudi airports and energy infrastructure, including a reported strike near Dammam that killed two people and injured eight. Saudi Aramco instructed staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters and work remotely following the latest security incidents.

The attacks in the Strait of Hormuz have intensified recently after Iran said in early October that it would close illegal routes used by the US to escort vessels through the strait. The IRGC claimed yesterday that it attacked four vessels and three others struck naval mines. This morning, Iran claimed that the illicit vessel traffic in Hormuz stopped after the continued attacks.

Looking ahead, crude oil remains supported amid the tensions in the Middle East and the prospects of another US attack against Iran after the midterms. Unless we get a de-escalation in the Saudi-Houthi conflict or a surprising breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations, oil prices will likely continue to rise.

If the price gets there, we can expect the sellers to step in, with a defined risk above the resistance, to position for a drop back into the lower bound of the channel.

item.title: Bitcoin erases all the weekly gains as growth concerns lead to widespread risk aversion. What's next?
item.description:

The risk-off flows started late Wednesday following reports that the US military was reducing its troop presence at bases in the Middle East, while the State Department ordered staff cuts at diplomatic posts amid rising security risks and the possibility of renewed military action against Iran.

The selling pressure then intensified after The New York Times reported that the US and Israeli militaries had developed detailed plans for potential strikes on Iran following the US midterm elections. The report also said that the US was building up its military presence which is expected to be fully deployed by early November.

The prospects of another direct conflict between the US and Iran amid increasing growth concerns and a hawkish Fed are all strong bearish drivers for the crypto market.

The focus today will be on the US Flash PMIs as it could be another major catalyst given the growth concerns.  Weaker-than-expected data could intensify growth fears, weigh further on risk sentiment and trigger another selloff in Bitcoin. Strong data, on the other hand, could alleviate fears in the near-term and lead to a relief rally, although it wouldn’t change the bigger picture.

item.title: UK October flash services PMI 53.1 vs 51.8 expected
item.description:
• Prior 52.1
  • Manufacturing PMI 52.8 vs 51.7 expected
  • Prior 51.9
  • Composite PMI 53.1 vs 51.8 expected
  • Prior 52.0

Key findings:

Business activity growth accelerates to its fastest since February, helped by rebound in new orders

Comment:

Chris Williamson, Chief Business Economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence:

“The UK economy has picked up momentum in October, with early PMI data indicating the strongest rate of growth since February. This encouraging sign of economic resilience is underscored by firms taking on additional workers for the first time since hiring was hit by the 2024 Autumn Budget.

"There are reports of paused spending due to a lack of clarity on domestic economic policy in the run up to the Budget, meaning the promising economic picture from the latest PMIs should provide an encouraging base for further robust economic growth through the winter months, barring any adverse surprises to businesses in the tax and spending review.

"Geopolitics, and notably the potential for conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine to add to energy market volatility, are, however, clearly still unsettling many businesses, and cost of living concerns and broader fiscal worries are being compounded by the shift to higher borrowing costs.

"Price pressures remain worryingly elevated, not only making a rate hike from the Bank of England at its upcoming policy meeting a near certainty but also likely shortening the odds of further rate hikes into 2027.”

The UK economy showed renewed strength in October, with the Composite PMI rising to 53.1 from 52.0 in September, its highest level since February. Business activity accelerated across both manufacturing and services, while new orders expanded at the fastest pace in 25 months and employment returned to growth for the first time since September 2024.

This contrasts with the loss of momentum across the eurozone. The divergence in economic performance has been supporting the british pound against the euro, with EUR/GBP extending the decline after the positive UK PMIs.

Chart: EUR/GBP - 4 hour timeframe

The data also reinforces expectations for BoE rate hikes as the central bank will have to lean against the inflationary pressures. Input cost inflation accelerated to its strongest pace since June, driven largely by higher energy prices. Although prices charged by businesses increased at a slightly slower pace, the resilient economic activity, stronger new orders and renewed employment growth gives the BoE less room to be patient and look through the shock.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold gets caught in market liquidation despite falling real yields supporting higher prices
item.description:
Gold extended the losses yesterday after breaking below the 4,070 support as widespread risk aversion tightened financial conditions. It looks like gold have been driven mainly by liquidations to cover losses in the stock market, much like what we’ve seen in 2025.  

To understand the mechanics, imagine that an investment fund holds stocks, gold and government bonds. Some stocks suddenly crash, and the fund suffers losses on leveraged positions. The fund may need to raise cash to meet margin calls, reduce leverage or satisfy investor redemptions. Rather than selling only the assets that caused the losses, it may sell whatever it can liquidate quickly. Gold is particularly useful in this situation because it is highly liquid and can be sold quickly.

The main drivers like real yields have been actually pointing to higher gold prices. In fact, real yields fell significantly as inflation expectations remain roughly unchanged given the increase in oil prices, while nominal Treasury yields fell due to growth concerns. This might be an opportunity for the buyers to fade the weakness and enter at better prices.

Today, the focus will be on the US Flash PMIs. If the data surprises to the downside, growth concerns will likely intensify, and we should get another dovish repricing. In this scenario, gold should be supported as real yields would fall further. Stronger than expected data, on the other hand, could quell growth fears in the near-term and put renewed pressure on gold.

 

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that gold(CFD contract) extended the losses yesterday after breaking below the 4,070 support. We are approaching a key support zone around the 3,885 level where we have also a major upward trendline for confluence. If the price gets there, we can expect the buyers to step in, with a defined risk below the trendline, to position for a rally into new record highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break lower to increase the bearish bets into the 3,500 level next.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we can see more clearly the selloff after the price broke below the 4,070 support as more sellers piled in to target the 3,885 level. If we get a pullback before that, we can expect the sellers to step in again around the 4,070 resistance, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to extend the pullback into the downward trendline next.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor downward trendline defining the bearish momentum. The sellers will likely continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into the 3,885 support. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to pile in for a pullback into the major downward trendline, with the 4,070 resistance as the first target. item.title: Eurozone October PMI misses estimates as growth slows, keeping ECB rate hike dilemma alive
item.description:
• Eurozone October flash services PMI 51.7 vs 52.5 expected
  • Prior 53.0
  • Eurozone October flash manufacturing PMI 52.4 vs 52.7 expected
  • Prior 52.9
  • Eurozone October flash composite PMI 51.9 vs 52.7 expected
  • Prior 53.1

After the softer prints from France and Germany, the weaker-than-expected results for the overall euro area are not all too surprising. But at least for now, business activity continues to grow with both output and new orders increasing for the fourth successive month in October, albeit at the slowest pace during this sequence.

A key drag on growth was a renewed drop in business activity in the French services sector. But there were also signs of weakness elsewhere in the region as growth also edged lower in the rest of the euro area for both the manufacturing and services sectors.

Looking to prices, manufacturers reported a sharp and accelerated increase in input prices in October amid higher energy costs mostly. The latest rise was the steepest since May and above the average for the year-to-date. However, the rate of output price inflation slowed in October at least with both Germany and France posting weaker increases in selling prices than in September. As for the rest of the euro area, they saw the rate of inflation accelerate as a whole.

Overall, the data pretty much underscores that higher interest rates are also starting to take a toll and dampening demand. But the picture of sustained growth and more stubborn inflation pressures will likely add to speculation of more aggressive policy tightening from the ECB down the road.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: European stock market open: Stocks slip as weak French PMI adds to economic worries
item.description:
• Eurostoxx -0.3%
  • Germany DAX -0.5%
  • France CAC 40 -0.6%
  • UK FTSE -0.2%
  • Spain IBEX -0.1%
  • Italy FTSE MIB flat

European indices are opening slightly lower across the board as the more cautious risk mood carries over from yesterday. The selling pressure isn't quite as intense for now, but there's little reason for investors to be feeling too optimistic either.

The selloff in Wall Street yesterday continues to cast a shadow over broader sentiment, with concerns surrounding AI-related stocks and elevated oil prices keeping investors on edge. US futures are also looking more tepid today, with S&P 500 futures down 0.1% for the time being.

And to kick start the session, economic data isn't offering much comfort either. France's October flash PMI figures were a notable disappointment, with the composite reading falling to 48.4 from 51.1 in September. That puts the French private sector back into contraction, as both manufacturing and services activity deteriorated amid weakening demand and heightened political uncertainty.

That being said, I wouldn't read too much into the French numbers alone just yet. Germany and the Eurozone PMI releases are still to come, and those will offer a better indication of whether the slowdown is spreading more widely.

For European stocks though, the concern is that weakening growth prospects are now adding to an already uncomfortable backdrop of higher bond yields, fiscal uncertainty, and a more fragile global risk sentiment.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Germany October flash manufacturing PMI 54.2 vs 53.5 expected
item.description:
• Prior 53.9
  • Services PMI 51.7 vs 52.5 expected
  • Prior 52.9
  • Composite PMI 52.8 vs 53.3 expected
  • Prior 53.8

Key findings: 

Economic activity softens in October

Comment:

Phil Smith, Economics Associate Director at S&P Global Market Intelligence:

"October's flash PMI results encouragingly showed a sustained upturn in business activity across Germany, although a slowdown in growth underscored that the recovery in the eurozone's largest economy remains fragile. Inflows of new work rose only modestly and at the slowest rate for three months at the start of the fourth quarter, with a stalling of new business growth in the service sector highlighting the ongoing headwinds to demand from elevated inflation and uncertainty.

"Labour market conditions continue to show a very gradual improvement, reflecting a steady but modest pace of job creation among services providers alongside an increasingly stable picture in the manufacturing sector.

"Whilst goods producers continued to see business conditions improve, aided by sustained growth in export sales and the filtering through of increased defence and infrastructure spending, a renewed surge in cost pressures has dampened expectations across the sector, with the two likely to remain intrinsically linked in the months ahead."

The market is being proved right as the PMIs are showing a slowdown in economic activity. Germany’s private sector continued to expand in October, but the pace of economic activity slowed noticeably, with the Composite PMI falling to 52.8 from 53.8 in September. Although the index remained above the 50 threshold separating expansion from contraction, the slowdown was broad-based, with both manufacturing output and services activity losing momentum. New business growth also eased to a three-month low, while demand in the services sector stalled amid delayed customer decisions and tighter client budgets.

The outlook for the coming months also points to increasing downside risks. Manufacturing firms reported a notable deterioration in business confidence, with expectations falling to their lowest since July as rising oil prices and raw material costs intensified concerns about margins and future activity. Meanwhile, the weakness in services demand and the slowdown in new orders could weigh on output growth if businesses become more cautious about spending and hiring.

The combination of weaker French and German PMIs led to a dovish repricing for the ECB as expectations for further tightening in light of an economic slowdown are getting challenged. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: France October PMI slumps back into contraction as political uncertainty weighs on demand
item.description:
• France October flash services PMI 48.4 vs 50.7 expected
  • Prior 51.2
  • France October flash manufacturing PMI 49.3 vs 50.5 expected
  • Prior 50.6
  • France October flash composite PMI 48.4 vs 50.5 expected
  • Prior 51.1

That's not a good sign as the French private sector falls back into contraction in October, amid political and financial concerns. Weighing on activity levels was the sharpest decline in demand for French goods and services since May, which surveyed businesses attributed to heightened uncertainty and economic pressures.

The only good news perhaps for the ECB is that the survey's price gauges decreased from September to signal an easing of input cost and output charge inflation rates.

Looking at the breakdown, manufacturers and service providers reported steeper declines in demand amid reports of projects being postponed as customers held back on decision making. Meanwhile, French businesses turned pessimistic towards one-year outlook with the future composite index falling to its lowest level since April 2020. That indicates negative corporate sentiment for the first time in close to two years. The more downbeat expectations were often linked to next year's election period, with some companies also expressing concerns regarding public finances.

On prices, data at the composite level signalled an easing of inflation across France in October. The service sector was the main driver, with slower rates of input cost and output charge inflation offsetting sharper price pressures for manufacturers.

Overall, the report today does at least put economic expectations and inflation pressures in sync. Both are coming in a little softer and may tone down ECB rate hike expectations. But again, this is only France - who is already facing up against big troubles from a fiscal and economic standpoint. We still have to see how the PMI numbers play out with Germany and the rest of the euro area for better confirmation.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: UK retail sales fall more than expected in September, complicating BOE rate hike outlook
item.description:
• UK September retail sales -0.4% vs -0.1% m/m expected
  • Prior +0.5; revised to +0.7%
  • UK September retail sales +0.8% vs +1.0% y/y expected
  • Prior +2.4%; revised to +2.7%
  • UK September retail sales (ex autos, fuel) -0.7% vs -0.1% m/m expected
  • Prior +0.6%; revised to +0.9%
  • UK September retail sales (ex autos, fuel) +0.8% vs +1.5% y/y expected
  • Prior +2.7%; revised to +2.9%

UK retail sales disappointed in September, falling by 0.4% on the month and missing expectations of a 0.1% decline. That comes after a stronger revision to the August number, which saw a 0.7% increase. Having said that, the quarterly picture is still holding up reasonably well as retail sales volumes rose by 0.7% in Q3 compared with the previous quarter.

Looking at the details, the weakness was fairly broad. Supermarket sales declined after gains in the previous two months, while non-food store sales volumes fell by 0.4%. Clothing retailers also struggled, with the unusually warm September weather weighing on demand for autumn and winter collections.

However, there are also signs that consumers are becoming more cautious with some retailers pointing to lower footfall and customers cutting back on spending.

Coming into the report, markets have been pricing in roughly 98% odds of a November rate hike, with December sitting closer to 45%. The numbers today will not do much to derail expectations for November, especially after the recent inflation figures. But they certainly make the argument for another move in December less straightforward, with the pricing there being more or less a coin flip at this stage.

The BOE has a tough balancing act to manage at the moment. Inflation remains stubborn, while the labour market and now consumer spending are offering less reassurance about the strength of the economy.

So for now, November still looks firmly on the table. But beyond that, the retail sales release today gives policymakers another reason to proceed more cautiously.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Falling Treasury yields may be hiding a darker story about the AI boom
item.description:
Let's take a step back and check on the key market drivers this week. The US-Iran conflict is still raging on and geopolitical tensions remain high. So, that is underpinning oil prices once again with WTI crude breaching $100 and Brent crude hitting $114 - its highest since May.

Now, that sounds like a familiar backdrop for the bond market, doesn't it? Higher oil prices mean stronger inflation pressures, which should normally push up Treasury yields. Well, that has not been the case this week.

Instead, Treasury yields have fallen sharply, with 10-year yields even slipping back below the 5% threshold in overnight trading and holding thereabouts since. But wait a second, shouldn't falling yields then buy some relief for stocks?

You would certainly think so, especially when surging Treasury yields have been such a major bane for equities over the past two months. And yet stocks have been battered this week, with AI names in particular bearing the brunt of the pain. So, what gives?

It's one thing to suggest that investors are perhaps starting to worry about growth conditions again. But considering how long that narrative has been brushed aside and the extent of the damage we are seeing in AI stocks, I think there is perhaps a rather different problem brewing beneath the surface.

Let's jump straight into it and start with CoreWeave, shall we?

That's not the most familiar name in the AI space. However, CoreWeave might well have been the stone that started an avalanche of worries about debt financing in the entire sector.

Just take a look at the chart below, which shows how the cost of insuring against defaults among major AI-related companies has surged over the past year i.e. change in CDS spreads.

The chart might seem complicated at first glance but the underlying message is quite straightforward. And that is investors are becoming more nervous about lending money to companies involved in the AI boom.

CoreWeave stands out like a sore thumb, with its CDS spread widening by more than 500 basis points over the observed period. But what exactly does that mean?

The simple way to think about it is to picture CDS as an insurance that investors can buy to protect themselves against a company failing to repay its debt. So, a five-year CDS provides that protection over five years and the spread simply reflects the cost of obtaining it. To give more context, 100 bps equals to 1% annually.

As such, when CoreWeave's actual five-year CDS spread surged to above 1,000 bps last week, that implied roughly $100,000 annually to insure $1 million of debt. Now, that's an enormous premium to pay just to protect yourself against a potential default.

And while CoreWeave is clearly the standout, the chart also shows that the worries aren't confined to just one company. Oracle's five-year CDS has climbed towards 300 bps, while Meta and Nvidia have seen theirs approach 100 bps.

In the case of Oracle, it is being traded like junk credit due to aggressive debt-fueled infrastructure loans. Meanwhile, the five-year CDS level for Meta is near its historic peak so that helps to put things into better perspective. Having said that, I wouldn't put all these companies in the same risk category. Meta and Nvidia clearly have much stronger financial positions and liquidity than CoreWeave for example.

However, it is clear that investors are beginning to question something bigger. And that brings us back to the same question we've been asking all year, that is who is going to pay for the enormous AI infrastructure boom, and how long before those investments generate sufficient returns?

CoreWeave relies heavily on debt to finance data centres and computing infrastructure. Meanwhile, Oracle is also committing massive sums to AI expansion and Meta is also pouring billions into infrastructure. As for Nvidia, their fortunes are very much closely tied to that spending cycle.

The major concern here is that if financing becomes more expensive or AI investment slows, the consequences could spread across companies that depend on one another for revenues, financing and growth.

So, what does this have to do with the bond market and Treasury yields?

Considering the backdrop above, investors are essentially growing more uncomfortable in wanting to hold riskier corporate debt and equities. So, what other options do they have left that pays a safe and good return in this market? Well, the answer is quite simply government bonds. And that pushes Treasury prices higher and yields lower as the demand flows in.

But then, here's the catch though. Even if Treasury yields fall, corporate borrowing costs can still rise when investors demand a bigger premium for taking on credit risk. In other words, safer money is getting cheaper while riskier money is becoming more expensive.

And that might explain why tech stocks aren't able to celebrate the sharp fall in Treasury yields. Investors may be worrying more about financing risks and future profits than the immediate benefit of cheaper government borrowing.

With all that said, AI credit concerns aren't necessarily the only reason Treasuries are rallying. However, they are likely one part of the picture that could be helpful in explaining the market moves we're seeing this week.

I mean, with inflation risks still lingering and oil prices elevated, falling Treasury yields aren't exactly hinting at better economic conditions. It could simply be investors starting to worry that something else might break first instead.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trade Tech Solutions Launches Perpetual Futures Prop Firm Technology as Platform Surpasses 2 Million Users

item.title: Heads up: UK retail sales to test the case for further BOE rate hikes
item.description:
The UK retail sales release will be one of the main items to watch out for in the economic calendar today, especially after the latest inflation and labour market figures have given the BOE plenty to think about ahead of its November meeting.

For the September report, retail sales are expected to fall by 0.1% on the month, following a 0.5% increase in August. Meanwhile, retail sales are expected to rise by 1.0% annually - a slowdown from 2.4% previously. The numbers might not be all too interesting on the surface, but they will matter to the broader context in shaping the BOE outlook.

UK headline annual inflation climbed to 3.5% in September, with core annual inflation also picking up to 2.8%. That is hardly reassuring for the BOE, especially with policymakers already having to contend with elevated energy prices and the risk of more persistent price pressures.

Meanwhile, the labour market gave us a bit of a surprise earlier this week. The unemployment rate surprisingly fell to 4.7%, while real wage growth nudged slightly higher to 3.7%. The numbers might be affected by data quality issues with the ONS but they reflect a modest bounce in labour market conditions regardless. Having said that, the details are less rosy with job vacancies continuing to decline, suggesting that hiring demand is losing momentum.

And in any case, one report doesn't make a trend. The UK labour market has been showing signs of softness this year and I would be remiss if I didn't point out that fact.

So, it's not to say everything is pointing to one direction for the BOE. The central bank still has a balancing act to manage.

On one hand, more stubborn inflation pressures are making a stronger case for tighter monetary policy. But on the other, a cooling jobs market and weaker consumer spending could raise concerns that the economy is struggling to cope with higher prices and borrowing costs.

So, what can we expect from the retail sales release today?

As things stand, traders are pricing in roughly 98% odds of a rate hike in November. Meanwhile, the probability of another move in December is sitting at around 45%.

Now, I don't think the retail sales numbers today will do much of anything to change the outlook for November - even on any major surprises. Markets are already firmly positioned for the rate hike and policymakers have done little to dissuade traders from that narrative.

But for December? That is where things could get interesting as the odds are more or less a coin flip at this stage.

A stronger-than-expected report would reinforce the argument that consumer demand remains resilient enough for the BOE to keep tightening. On the flip side, a big disappointment could cast further doubt on how much more tightening the economy can withstand at this juncture.

So, that is the more important takeaway when viewing the retail sales release today. It's all about looking to see how this might affect the December outlook or even for next year.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.description:

  • OpenAI close to raising up to $30 billion at $1.25 trillion valuation, UAE investors lead
  • Japan CPI preview: core seen at 2.1%, topping BoJ target for first time since December

Summary:

  • Asian equities mostly fell after Thursday’s US chip sell-off: South Korea’s KOSDAQ dropped 3.5%, the Kospi 2.2%, the Nikkei 1.4% and the Shanghai Composite 1.3%, while the Hang Seng edged up 0.25%.
  • Gold traded below $4,000 an ounce for the first time since July but did not extend its losses.
  • Oil traded in a narrow range near recent highs, after Brent closed at its highest since May on Thursday.
  • Major currencies were range-bound, with the yen firming modestly after Japan’s inflation data.
  • Japan’s core CPI rose 2.1% in September, back above the BoJ’s target, and the measure excluding fresh food and fuel beat forecasts at 2.4%. Japan’s flash PMI held at 52.3.
  • Australia’s flash composite PMI fell into contraction for the first time in five months.
  • In company news, OpenAI is reportedly near a $30 billion raise, SK hynix dropped plans for a US Solidigm IPO, and Western Digital posted a sharp revenue jump.

Equities

Asian stock markets mostly fell on Friday as a sell-off in US semiconductor shares spread to the region. South Korean markets, which have heavy weightings in chipmakers, led the declines: the tech-focused KOSDAQ fell 3.5% and the benchmark Kospi lost 2.2%. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 1.4% and China’s Shanghai Composite fell 1.3%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng was the exception, edging up 0.25%.

The losses followed a sharp fall on Wall Street on Thursday, when the Philadelphia semiconductor index dropped 6.7%, its biggest daily decline since June. The Nasdaq fell more than 2.5% after earnings from major technology companies, including Meta’s spending plans, renewed concerns about returns on AI investment.

Oil

Oil prices traded in a narrow range in Asian hours, holding near recent highs. Brent crude closed around $113 a barrel on Thursday, its highest level since early May, after reports that the US and Israel had drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month’s US midterm elections.

Supply concerns in fuel markets also remained in focus. President Donald Trump invoked the Defense Production Act for domestic oil production and refining as high fuel prices weigh on voters ahead of the November 3 elections. Separately, Bloomberg reported that Russia’s Rosneft is deliberately slowing repairs at refineries damaged by repeated Ukrainian drone strikes, which could keep Russian fuel exports constrained.

Gold

Gold fell below $4,000 an ounce for the first time since July, though it did not follow through lower in Asian trading. There was no fresh catalyst for the move. The metal has been pressured by elevated bond yields, a firm dollar and expectations of further Federal Reserve tightening tied to high oil prices. It is now roughly a quarter below its January peak of more than $5,400. Longer-term support continues to come from central bank buying and investors seeking diversification.

FX

Major currency pairs were range-bound. The yen firmed modestly after Japan’s inflation data. USD/JPY dropped to around 156.25 before recovering back to 157.00. 

Japan

Japan’s core consumer inflation rose 2.1% in September from a year earlier, matching forecasts and accelerating from 1.7% in August. It was the first reading above the BoJ’s 2% target in nine months. A measure excluding fresh food and fuel, which the central bank watches closely, rose 2.4%, above forecasts of 2.3%. Goods and services inflation both accelerated, despite government fuel subsidies.

The BoJ is widely expected to keep rates at 1.25% at its meeting ending October 30, though it may raise its inflation forecasts. Many analysts expect a hike to 1.50% in December. Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi said conditions have not yet been met for the government to declare an end to deflation.

Japan’s flash composite PMI was unchanged at 52.3 in October. Services activity strengthened, while manufacturing output grew at its slowest pace in seven months. Job creation slowed to a 14-month low, and input cost inflation edged higher.

Australia

Australia’s flash composite PMI fell to 47.7 in October from 51.3, signalling the first contraction in private sector output in five months. Services activity declined for the first time since May, as firms cited weaker confidence, higher borrowing costs and inflation pressures. Input costs rose at the fastest pace since May, and businesses continued to pass higher costs on to customers.

Company news

OpenAI is close to finalising a funding round of up to $30 billion at a pre-money valuation of $1.25 trillion, led by investors from the United Arab Emirates, according to reports. The valuation is below the roughly $1.4 trillion the company had reportedly sought earlier this month.

SK hynix said its Solidigm unit has ended a review of a US initial public offering, citing market conditions and share price trends. The listing had been considered to help fund a new US plant. SK hynix shares fell as much as 4.2% in early Seoul trading before swinging between gains and losses.

Western Digital reported fiscal first-quarter revenue up about 55% to $4.38 billion, driven by AI-related storage demand and higher prices, and guided above forecasts for the current quarter. Its shares nonetheless fell in after-hours trading amid the broader sell-off in AI-linked stocks. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: HSBC’s RedCoin stablecoin goes live in Hong Kong: what the launch answers, and what it still doesn’t
item.description:
HSBC has started rolling out RedCoin, its Hong Kong dollar-backed stablecoin, to more than 3.3 million users of its PayMe payments app, according to the South China Morning Post. The phased launch began on Friday, 23 October, starting with transfers between users and payments to merchants. Three weeks ago, investingLive flagged that RedCoin had a name but no launch date. That question now has an answer. Two others do not: which blockchain RedCoin runs on, and whether it can ever leave HSBC’s own apps.

What happened

According to the SCMP, PayMe users can activate a RedCoin wallet with no minimum balance and no extra account-opening steps. Once they update the app, they can select the wallet and send money instantly, through an interface similar to the existing PayMe experience. Full availability is expected before the weekend.

Lawrence Li, head of PayMe, told the paper the first phase is about keeping the service stable, avoiding extra hassle for customers and earning their trust. That is a deliberately cautious start for a bank-issued token.

The SCMP also reported that HSBC plans to add RedCoin to its Hong Kong mobile banking app by year-end. That would allow instant subscriptions to tokenised money market funds from HK$100, with tokenised gold and third-party funds to follow.

HSBC is one of only two firms licensed to issue stablecoins in Hong Kong. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority granted the first issuer licences on 10 April to HSBC and to Anchorpoint Financial, a joint venture of Standard Chartered Hong Kong, HKT and Animoca Brands. Anchorpoint began a phased rollout of its own HKDAP stablecoin in August.

Why this stablecoin is different

A stablecoin is a digital token designed to hold a steady value, usually backed one-for-one by a traditional currency and reserve assets. HSBC says RedCoin will be redeemable one-for-one for Hong Kong dollars and backed by segregated assets.

The best-known stablecoins, such as USDT and USDC, are issued by crypto companies and move freely between wallets and exchanges. RedCoin is issued by a licensed bank and, for now, can only be used inside HSBC’s own apps.

That difference matters. If RedCoin stays inside PayMe and the HSBC app, users may notice little change from today’s PayMe balances: the difference is mostly in the plumbing underneath. If it later becomes transferable to outside wallets, it would be much closer to a crypto-style stablecoin, with a major bank standing behind it.

What we flagged in September, and where it stands

  • Launch date: answered. RedCoin is live in phases from 23 October.
  • Blockchain: still not disclosed in reporting so far.
  • External wallets: still not addressed.
  • Scale: the 3.3 million figure, which we earlier traced to an unnamed outlet, is now reported by the SCMP as PayMe’s user base. That is the number of people who can use RedCoin, not the number who will.

Why it matters, and what it doesn’t change

The launch is an early test of whether regulated, bank-issued stablecoins can win everyday use, and of Hong Kong’s push to become a regulated hub for digital assets. The planned link to tokenised funds from HK$100 is the more significant step for investors. It would give ordinary retail customers a route into tokenised assets, which is where stablecoins connect to the wider tokenisation trend.

It does not directly affect Bitcoin or Ether, and RedCoin is not a token traders can buy on an exchange. As we noted in September, the HKMA has warned about fraudulent tokens. Anything trading under the RedCoin or HSBC name on a crypto exchange is not the bank’s product.

What could change the interpretation

The story strengthens if HSBC discloses the blockchain, opens RedCoin to outside wallets, reports solid activation numbers or delivers the tokenised fund link on schedule. It weakens if uptake is slow, the first phase runs into technical problems, or RedCoin remains a closed system that adds little to what PayMe already does.

What to watch next

  • Activation figures. How many of the 3.3 million eligible users actually switch on a RedCoin wallet.
  • Blockchain and wallet access. These are the two disclosures that decide what kind of stablecoin RedCoin really is.
  • The year-end app integration. Watch whether tokenised money market funds from HK$100 arrive on time.
  • HKDAP comparison. Anchorpoint’s rollout is the only like-for-like benchmark in Hong Kong.

The practical takeaway: RedCoin is now real, but for the moment it is a payments upgrade inside HSBC’s apps rather than a new crypto asset. The disclosures still to come will show whether it becomes more than that.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold drops below $4,000 for first time since July as yields and dollar weigh
item.description:
The $4,000 break matters more as a psychological level than as a reaction to news, and losing it could trigger further selling from momentum-driven and leveraged holders. The most important near-term link runs through oil: Brent above $110 a barrel keeps inflation expectations high, which supports further Fed tightening, higher Treasury yields and a firm dollar, all of which weigh on a metal that pays no interest. The Fed decision on October 28 is the next major test. A hawkish message would likely add pressure, while any sign of a pause could give gold room to recover. Equity volatility is also a risk: further sharp falls in tech shares could force more selling of gold to meet margin calls, as happened during Thursday’s chip sell-off.

--

Gold has slipped below $4,000 without a single trigger, pushed down by yields, the dollar and forced selling, while the long-term buyers who drove its rally have not left the market.

Summary:

  • Gold fell below $4,000 an ounce in Asian trading on Friday, its first move under that level since July, without a specific news catalyst.
  • The metal is now roughly a quarter below its peak above $5,400 an ounce in January.
  • Pressure is coming from elevated real yields, a strong dollar and expectations of further Fed tightening tied to high oil prices.
  • Gold has also been sold during equity sell-offs as leveraged investors raise cash to meet margin calls.
  • Longer-term support comes from central bank reserve diversification, ETF inflows, new institutional buyers in China and India, and concerns over debt and inflation.
  • The Fed decision on October 28 is the next major test for the market.

Gold fell below $4,000 an ounce in Asian trading on Friday for the first time since July, extending a slide that has taken the metal roughly a quarter below its January peak of more than $5,400. There was no fresh catalyst. Instead, the move reflects steady pressure from the same macro forces that have weighed on bullion for most of the year.

The biggest factor is the rising cost of holding gold. Strategists at HSBC said earlier this year that US Treasury yields have become the main driver of the gold price: when yields rise, holding an asset that pays no interest becomes more expensive. Yields have stayed elevated as high energy prices from the Middle East conflict keep inflation concerns alive and support expectations of further Federal Reserve tightening, after the Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023. A strong dollar adds to the pressure by making gold more expensive for buyers outside the US. MUFG expects the dollar to remain stronger for longer, forecasting only a gradual decline through 2027.

Gold has also lost some of its traditional appeal as a hedge. It has not rallied during the Middle East conflict and has largely moved in line with equities this year, HSBC noted. Its asset management strategists said recently that leveraged money crowded into gold means sharp stock market falls trigger margin calls, forcing investors to sell bullion to raise cash. That pattern appeared again this week, when gold fell sharply on the same day a slump in chip stocks pulled the Nasdaq down more than 2.5%.

HSBC’s chief precious metals analyst, James Steel, has argued that this selling is not evidence that gold has failed. In his view, when oil rose, inflation fears returned and stocks fell, investors needed cash and gold provided it, effectively cashing in an insurance policy rather than abandoning it. He also suggested the January rally had drawn in a lot of new money and left the market overly long, which means part of the decline may reflect a necessary reset in positioning.

The supports for gold are long term rather than immediate. Central banks continue to diversify their reserves into bullion, and HSBC has pointed to steady inflows into exchange-traded funds. Regulatory changes have opened the market to large new institutional buyers, allowing major Chinese insurers and Indian asset managers to hold gold, and Steel has noted that Chinese demand has shifted towards larger institutional bars. Concerns over government debt and inflation also continue to support the so-called debasement trade, in which investors move into hard assets. HSBC’s asset management team said the strategic case for holding gold remains intact despite the recent weakness.

The balance therefore depends on time horizon. In the near term, yields, the dollar and forced selling are dominating, and the $4,000 level has now given way. Over a longer horizon, structural demand from central banks and new institutional investors provides a base that was not as strong in earlier downturns.

What would change the picture is a turn in rates. A softer message from the Fed on October 28, a pullback in Treasury yields or easing oil prices would reduce the cost of holding gold and could allow structural buyers to regain control. Conversely, a hawkish Fed, a further rise in yields or more turbulence in equities would likely keep pressure on the metal, with the debate shifting to how far below $4,000 it can fall before longer-term buyers step in.

item.title: Three AI listings stalled in a month: the money behind the AI boom is getting pickier
item.description:
The squeeze is likely to widen the gap within the AI trade. Cash-generating hyperscalers and established suppliers can fund spending internally, while newer, debt- or equity-reliant players face higher costs and a narrower window. Credit is the market to watch: spreads on high-yield AI infrastructure debt, led by CoreWeave, are the earliest warning of whether stress is spreading or staying contained. In Asia, Korean and Taiwanese chip stocks are highly sensitive to any slowdown in AI capital spending, a risk already reflected in SK hynix’s roughly halved market value since June. Oil is part of the cost-of-capital story: Brent above $110 a barrel keeps inflation and rate expectations high, keeping bond yields elevated and raising the hurdle for capital-intensive projects whose payback is years away.

---

Demand for AI hardware remains strong, but investors are becoming much more selective about how they fund it, and the companies most dependent on outside capital are feeling it first.

Summary:

  • Three AI-linked listings have been cancelled, halted or delayed this month: Firmus Grid’s roughly $5 billion IPO, Airtrunk’s Singapore listing and SK hynix’s planned Solidigm IPO.
  • OpenAI is reportedly near a funding round of up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation, below the roughly $1.4 trillion it initially sought.
  • Debt markets are flashing stress, with yields on some of CoreWeave’s unsecured debt around 15%.
  • The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell 6.7% on Thursday, its worst day since June, as Meta’s capital spending renewed doubts about returns on AI investment.
  • Counter-evidence remains strong: JPMorgan says positioning is largely washed out and the tech sector is generating about $400 billion more in cash than it spends, while Western Digital reported surging demand and prices.
  • Upcoming tests include megacap earnings, the Fed decision and SK hynix results on October 28, OpenAI’s funding round and Anthropic’s expected listing in mid-November.

The AI boom has not run out of demand, but it is running into a more cautious funding market. In the space of a few weeks, three planned listings linked to AI infrastructure have been cancelled, halted or delayed, private valuations have been marked below earlier targets, and parts of the debt market are pricing in genuine distress. Together, they suggest that investors who financed the build-out with few questions are becoming more selective.

The latest sign came on Friday, when SK hynix said its Solidigm unit had ended a review of a US initial public offering intended to help fund a new fabrication plant in the US. The South Korean chipmaker cited market conditions and share price trends, and said the decision did not reflect any change in Solidigm’s growth prospects. Reports earlier this autumn had suggested the listing could value the unit at up to $150 billion.

Solidigm followed two similar decisions in Asia-Pacific. Earlier this month, Australian data centre operator Firmus Grid cancelled an IPO of almost $5 billion that would have been the country’s largest in nearly 30 years, citing volatility. Days later, Blackstone-backed Airtrunk pushed a planned Singapore listing into the first half of next year, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The repricing extends to private markets. OpenAI is close to finalising a funding round of up to $30 billion at a pre-money valuation of $1.25 trillion, led by investors from the United Arab Emirates, according to reports this week. Earlier in October, Bloomberg reported the company had presented a valuation of about $1.4 trillion to investors as a fixed price. The new figure is still far above the roughly $850 billion valuation from March, but it suggests investors have pushed back on price. Reuters reported that OpenAI is rushing to secure commitments before rival Anthropic’s expected stock market debut in mid-November, as both draw on a similar pool of capital.

The strain is most visible in credit. CoreWeave, the largest of the neoclouds that rent computing power for AI workloads, has seen yields on some of its unsecured debt climb to around 15%, a level usually associated with distress, after heavy borrowing to build data centres. Analysts are divided. HSBC has flagged structural concerns across the neocloud sector, while Goldman Sachs argues CoreWeave’s use of asset-backed project financing limits the rise in its borrowing costs.

Public markets have reflected the same doubts. The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell 6.7% on Thursday, its biggest daily drop since June, and the Nasdaq slid more than 2.5% after earnings from major technology companies, including Meta’s spending plans, renewed concerns that the returns from AI may not justify the investment. SK hynix’s market value has roughly halved since its June peak.

Several forces are behind the change. Interest rates are rising: the Federal Reserve resumed hikes in September and the Bank of Japan has pushed its policy rate to a 31-year high. Higher rates make it more expensive to fund projects whose revenue arrives years after the spending. Geopolitical risk has also increased, with the war involving Iran keeping oil above $110 a barrel and inflation expectations elevated. And as the scale of AI spending has grown, investors have become more focused on when it will pay off.

There is a strong counter-argument. JPMorgan strategists said this week that hedge funds have already cut much of their exposure to chip stocks, which could limit further downside. They also noted that neocloud capital spending of about $80 billion this year is small next to roughly $1.8 trillion of total technology investment, and that the broader tech sector is generating about $400 billion more in cash than it spends, giving larger companies room to absorb any funding gaps. Demand also looks real: Western Digital said this week that revenue rose about 55% as AI customers drove a 28% rise in storage prices, and that it has demand visibility to 2030 or 2031 from its largest customers. OpenAI has told investors its annualised revenue has reached about $50 billion.

Taken together, the evidence points to a split rather than a collapse. Companies that can fund AI spending from their own cash flow remain well placed. Those that depend on external capital, especially debt-funded newcomers and new listings, face higher costs and tougher terms. That is a healthier sign of discipline than a reckless boom, but it also means growth may slow at the margin for the most leveraged parts of the supply chain.

Several tests are coming. Megacap earnings will show whether spending plans hold. The Fed decides on October 28, the same day SK hynix reports results. OpenAI’s round has yet to close, and Anthropic’s listing next month will show whether public investors are still willing to back AI at scale. A strong reception would suggest the window is reopening. Further pulled deals or wider spreads on AI-related debt would indicate the squeeze is deepening.  

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan’s 2.4% underlying inflation puts a higher BoJ terminal rate in play
item.description:
The debate is shifting from when the BoJ hikes again to where rates peak, which matters most for the front end of the JGB curve. A market that moves from pricing a terminal rate around 1.75% to one closer to or above 2% would be likely to push two-year and five-year yields higher after their recent rally. The yen firmed after the data, but a sustained rally would probably need the BoJ to endorse a higher peak next week, given the large trade deficit and the wide gap with US rates. For equities, a higher-for-longer BoJ path tends to favour banks over exporters. Oil remains the key upstream driver: Middle East-linked energy costs are feeding Japanese inflation even with fuel subsidies in place, so crude above $110 a barrel keeps upside risk on both prices and the BoJ’s forecasts.

---

Earlier:

  • Japan core inflation tops BoJ’s 2% target for first time since December, yen firms

---

Japan’s inflation is now broad enough that a December BoJ hike looks like the starting point rather than the question, with markets turning to how far the bank will ultimately need to go.

Summary:

  • Japan’s core CPI rose 2.1% in September from 1.7%, above the BoJ’s target for the first time in nine months. The measure excluding fresh food and fuel rose 2.4% from 1.9%.
  • Goods inflation rose to 2.8% from 2.6%, and services inflation rose to 1.5% from 1.2%, a sign that firms are passing on higher labour costs.
  • Higher fuel costs from the Middle East conflict, a weak yen and AI-driven demand are offsetting the effect of government fuel subsidies.
  • The BoJ is expected to hold rates at 1.25% next week but may raise its inflation forecasts and say underlying inflation has likely reached 2%.
  • Many analysts expect a hike to 1.50% in December, with a terminal rate around 1.75% to 2%, and some see the risk of a higher peak.
  • The PMI showed hiring slowing to a 14-month low, and the economy minister said conditions are not yet met to declare deflation over.

Japan’s underlying inflation accelerated in September, with price increases broadening across goods and services despite government fuel subsidies. The data strengthen expectations of a Bank of Japan rate hike in December and are shifting attention to how high rates may ultimately go.

Core consumer prices, which exclude fresh food but include fuel, rose 2.1% from a year earlier, matching forecasts and accelerating from 1.7% in August. It was the first reading above the BoJ’s 2% target in nine months, Reuters reported. The index excluding both fresh food and fuel, which the BoJ watches closely as a better measure of demand-driven inflation, rose 2.4% from 1.9%.

The breakdown showed price pressure spreading. Goods inflation rose to 2.8% from 2.6%, while services inflation increased to 1.5% from 1.2%, suggesting firms are starting to pass higher wages on to customers. Rising fuel costs linked to the prolonged Middle East conflict, higher import prices from a weak yen and strong demand linked to artificial intelligence have together blunted the impact of the fuel subsidies.

Services inflation remains the weak link in that picture. At 1.5%, it is still well short of 2%, a reminder that the wage-driven, domestically generated inflation the BoJ has long sought is building only gradually.

The BoJ is widely expected to keep its policy rate at 1.25% at its two-day meeting ending October 30, having raised it to a 31-year high in September. Sources have told Reuters the bank may revise up its inflation forecasts, signal that underlying inflation has likely reached 2%, and stress its focus on anchoring inflation at that level. Governor Kazuo Ueda said last week that the BoJ would not tolerate an inflation overshoot.

One economist told Reuters that rising energy costs and their knock-on effects should push core inflation higher, but that prices are not accelerating sharply enough to justify back-to-back hikes, and he expects the next move in December. Many analysts polled by Reuters expect the BoJ to raise rates to 1.50% in December, with a terminal rate of around 1.75% to 2%. Some see the risks tilting higher. Capital Economics said there is little evidence that tightening so far has slowed the economy and that the policy rate may peak above its 2% forecast. Recent surveys have shown little sign that higher rates are weighing on loan demand.

Not all of Friday’s data supported a more aggressive path. A flash business survey released the same morning showed private sector growth steady but subdued in October, with job creation slowing to a 14-month low and services firms cutting staff for the first time in more than a year. Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi said conditions have not yet been met for the government to declare an official end to deflation, and he urged the BoJ to guide policy appropriately.

That leaves the BoJ facing a familiar balance at next week’s meeting: inflation that is finally broadening, against signs that the labour market and domestic demand are losing some momentum. How the bank describes that balance in its outlook report is likely to shape market expectations for the policy rate well beyond December. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: What is blockchain finality? Why Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana settle at very different speeds
item.description:
When you send Bitcoin, Ether or SOL, the transaction shows up almost immediately. That doesn’t mean it is permanent. Every blockchain has a point after which a transaction can no longer be reversed, called finality, and the time it takes to get there ranges from under a second to around an hour depending on the network. Solana’s Alpenglow upgrade this week cut its finality time from about 12.8 seconds to a target of roughly 150 milliseconds, which makes this a good moment to explain what finality is and why traders should care.

What finality means

A blockchain is a shared record kept by thousands of computers that must agree on which transactions happened and in what order. Agreement takes time. Until enough of the network has signed off, there is a small chance a transaction could be dropped or replaced if part of the network had a different view of events.

Finality is the point where that chance is gone, or so small it can be ignored. Before it, a transaction is pending, however confident the screen looks. After it, the transaction is settled.

Bitcoin: finality by accumulation

Bitcoin never declares a transaction final. Instead, each new block added on top makes it harder to reverse, because rewriting history would mean redoing all the computing work in those later blocks. New blocks arrive about every 10 minutes on average.

This is called probabilistic finality. The longer you wait, the safer the transaction becomes. A common convention is to wait for six confirmations, roughly an hour, before treating a large payment as settled, though many exchanges credit deposits after fewer. The trade-off is clear: Bitcoin is slow to settle, but reversing a transaction buried under several blocks would require enormous computing power.

Ethereum: finality by checkpoint

Since its move to proof-of-stake, Ethereum has had a definite finality point. Validators, who lock up ETH to take part, vote on checkpoints. Once two-thirds of staked ETH has backed a checkpoint in two consecutive rounds, everything before it is finalized. Reversing a finalized block would mean a large share of validators losing their staked ETH.

In practice that takes about 15 minutes, according to ethereum.org. In a pleasing coincidence, the theoretical minimum is 12.8 minutes, the same figure as Solana’s old finality time, just in minutes rather than seconds. Faster finality is on Ethereum’s research roadmap, but there is no confirmed date.

Solana: finality in a fraction of a second

Solana also uses staked validators, but it is designed for speed. Under its previous system, TowerBFT, transactions were quickly marked “confirmed”, but full finality took about 12.8 seconds. Alpenglow, live on mainnet since 21 October, merges those stages into one and targets finality of about 150 milliseconds. Early dashboard readings have been somewhat above that target, so the real-world figure is worth watching as the network beds in. 

Why traders should care

Finality affects how quickly you can use your money. Exchanges usually wait for a transaction to settle before crediting a deposit, so slower finality means a longer wait before funds can be traded. For anyone moving coins between exchanges to take advantage of a price difference, that delay is a real cost, because the opportunity can disappear while the transfer settles.

It also matters for payments and decentralised finance. A merchant or lending app that acts on a transaction before it is final takes on a small risk that it gets reversed. Faster finality shrinks that window.

Speed is not the same as quality

It is tempting to read finality times as a league table, with Solana top and Bitcoin bottom. That misses the trade-offs. Bitcoin’s slower process is part of what makes its history so hard to rewrite. Ethereum’s longer window comes with a very large, widely distributed validator set. Solana’s speed relies on high-performance validators, and the network has a history of outages, so its new system still has to prove itself under real conditions over time.

The right question is not which network is fastest, but whether its settlement speed and security suit what you are doing. An hour is fine for moving savings into cold storage. It is not fine for a shop counter.

What to watch next

  • Exchange deposit times for SOL. If major exchanges cut their waiting periods, Alpenglow’s speed is reaching users.
  • Solana’s live finality. Watch whether it settles near the 150 millisecond target under heavy load.
  • Ethereum’s roadmap. Any firm timeline for faster finality would narrow the gap with faster networks.
  • Your own exchange’s policy. Check how many confirmations it needs for each coin before you move funds in a hurry.

The practical takeaway: a transaction on screen is not the same as a settled one. Knowing how long finality takes on each network tells you how long your money is really in transit.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan flash PMI holds at 52.3 as services gain offsets factory slowdown before BoJ
item.description:
The survey gives the BoJ a mixed but broadly workable backdrop: steady growth and persistent cost pressure support further policy normalisation, while weaker hiring and softer demand argue for a gradual pace. For the yen, the data are unlikely to shift expectations much on their own, coming alongside this morning’s above-forecast core-core CPI reading. In JGBs, the combination of solid activity and sticky input costs is consistent with the market keeping a December hike in play. For equities, the slowdown in manufacturing new orders and export business is a mild headwind for exporters. Raw material costs remain a key pressure point, and sustained high oil prices linked to the Middle East conflict are likely to keep input cost inflation elevated into year-end.

---

Earlier:

  • Japan core inflation tops BoJ’s 2% target for first time since December, yen firms

---

Japan’s private sector kept growing in October, but slowing factory momentum, weaker hiring and rising costs suggest the expansion is becoming more fragile as the BoJ weighs its next move.

Summary:

  • The S&P Global flash Japan composite PMI output index was unchanged at 52.3 in October, the 19th straight month of expansion but the joint-slowest pace since May.
  • Services activity rose to 52.0 from 51.3, while the manufacturing PMI fell to 53.3 from 54.1 and manufacturing output dropped to 53.1 from 54.9, a seven-month low.
  • New orders grew at the slowest pace in three months, led by the weakest rise in factory orders since March. New export business rose at the softest rate in four months.
  • Job creation slowed to a 14-month low, with services payrolls falling for the first time since August 2025, even as backlogs grew at the fastest pace since June.
  • Input cost inflation edged higher on raw material and labour costs, while output price inflation stayed sharp but slowed to a four-month low.
  • Business confidence fell to its lowest in three months, with inflation a key concern.

Japan’s private sector continued to expand in October, but growth remained subdued as a slowdown in manufacturing was offset by stronger services activity, according to flash survey data from S&P Global. Hiring slowed sharply and cost pressures increased, adding to the mixed picture facing the Bank of Japan ahead of next week’s policy meeting.

The S&P Global flash Japan composite PMI output index was unchanged at 52.3, marking the 19th consecutive month of growth but matching the slowest pace since May. Services business activity improved to 52.0 from 51.3, while manufacturing lost momentum. The headline manufacturing PMI fell to 53.3 from 54.1, and the factory output index dropped to 53.1 from 54.9, its weakest reading in seven months.

Demand softened. New business rose at the slowest pace in three months, as goods producers reported the weakest growth in new orders since March. Services sales growth picked up but remained modest. Foreign demand was still positive, though new export orders grew at the slowest rate in four months.

The labour market was a notable weak spot. Even though backlogs of work grew at the fastest pace since June, firms were cautious about adding staff, and job creation slowed to a 14-month low. Manufacturers increased their workforces moderately, but services companies cut payrolls for the first time since August 2025. Manufacturers also stepped up their purchasing, building inventories of inputs at the fastest rate in almost four years, while supplier delivery times lengthened substantially.

Price pressures remained a central theme. Input cost inflation edged higher and was marked overall, with firms pointing to higher raw material and labour costs. Companies continued to raise selling prices sharply, though the rate of output price inflation slowed to a four-month low. Businesses still expect output to be higher in a year’s time, but confidence fell to its lowest in three months, with inflation a key concern.

Usamah Bhatti, economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said overall growth was weaker than the average so far this year. He pointed to signs of a shift in momentum from manufacturing towards services as the year draws to a close. Bhatti described inflation as a key downside risk for the private sector and said it will be important to monitor domestic demand, given that the BoJ has raised its policy rate to 1.25%, the highest since 1995.

The survey was released shortly after national inflation data showed core inflation back above the BoJ’s 2% target in September, with the measure excluding food and energy rising faster than expected. Taken together, the data show an economy still growing and facing persistent cost pressures, but with signs of strain in hiring and demand.

Final October data are due on November 2 for manufacturing and November 5 for services and the composite index.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6758 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
